TFSA withdrawals and recontributions: draw the calendar before replacing the money

Four graphics separate account value, current contribution room, unplaced requests and the ordinary room restored when a new calendar year begins.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore a TFSA withdrawal and recontribution calendar

Ordinary hypothetical two-calendar-year TFSA ledger. Starting unused room is assumed already reconciled across all of the holder’s TFSAs, with Canadian residency and eligibility throughout. Contributions are capped at modeled available room; unplaced requests never enter an account. Withdrawal is capped at modeled value and does not restore same-year room. Year 2 adds unused room, the actual ordinary year-1 withdrawal and the entered new-dollar-room assumption. That assumption is not an official future-year limit or forecast. The central idea

An ordinary withdrawal reduces account value now and restores contribution room next calendar year. A same-year deposit still needs room that is already available.

01

Keep account value separate from contribution room

The CRA’s withdrawal guidance states that an ordinary TFSA withdrawal does not immediately create new available contribution room. The amount returns as room on January 1 of the next calendar year. Replacing money earlier requires unused room that is already available.

This calendar models a holder eligible and resident in Canada throughout both illustrated years. Starting room is assumed already reconciled across all of the holder’s TFSAs. It is entered separately from combined account value because one amount cannot be inferred from the other.

The model includes only the selected ordinary contributions and withdrawal, with no investment returns or other transactions. It excludes transfers, specified distributions, excess histories and non-resident periods. It is an explanation of one transaction sequence, rather than a statement of anyone’s actual room.

02

Follow what changes during the withdrawal year

The default starts with CAD 40,000 of combined account value and CAD 7,000 of unused room. The first requested CAD 5,000 contribution fits, raising value to CAD 45,000 and reducing available room to CAD 2,000.

The next event is a CAD 10,000 ordinary withdrawal. Account value falls to CAD 35,000, while available room remains CAD 2,000. The value and room bars therefore move differently at exactly the same event.

A later request to contribute CAD 10,000 is capped at the remaining CAD 2,000 in this model. That deposit raises value to CAD 37,000 and leaves no current-year room. The other CAD 8,000 of the request is marked unplaced; it never enters an account and is not modeled as an actual excess contribution.

03

Build the next-year room calculation from its components

When the new calendar year begins, the model adds unused room from the prior year, the ordinary withdrawal actually made, and a separate new-dollar-room assumption. Under the defaults, those components are zero, CAD 10,000 and CAD 7,000 respectively, producing CAD 17,000 before the next contribution.

The requested CAD 15,000 year-two deposit fits. Combined account value then reaches CAD 52,000, and unused room is CAD 2,000. The account-value check is opening value plus the three deposits actually placed, less the withdrawal actually made.

The new-year addition is an editable assumption, not an official future-year limit or a forecast. The CRA’s published table lists CAD 7,000 for 2026, but the applicable year, eligibility and transaction history must be checked for an actual calculation.

04

Read requests and accepted transactions separately

The contribution bars show the requested amount as a total, split between the deposit placed and the amount left out. This deliberately prevents the illustration from placing money beyond its simplified room calculation.

The withdrawal is also capped at the account value available at that event. A request above that amount does not create extra cash or additional restored room. The new-year waterfall uses the withdrawal actually modeled, rather than the original request.

The unplaced contribution amount is not a tax penalty, an investment loss or a balance in another account. The calendar assigns it no destination. A household budget needs its own record of where withdrawn or unplaced cash goes and whether a later contribution can be funded.

05

Use the matrix to isolate the same-year constraint

The matrix varies starting unused room and the later year-one contribution request. The first selected contribution still uses room before that later request. Each cell shows the amount of the later request that cannot be placed.

Changing the ordinary withdrawal cannot change this same-year result. It changes account value and the following year’s restoration instead. That distinction is the reason a withdrawal confirmation alone is insufficient evidence that the same amount can be contributed again immediately.

The CRA also explains that room applies collectively across a holder’s TFSAs and recommends reconciling records rather than relying only on a displayed account figure. Verify current room and transactions before making an actual deposit. These graphics make the ordinary timing visible without determining eligibility, calculating tax on excesses or replacing the holder’s full transaction ledger.
